name: Oats
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Oats (jai) is a useful, highly nutritious winter fodder that keeps growing in severe cold, good for both draught and milking animals; oat straw is more nutritious than wheat straw. It grows best in cool, humid weather and cannot stand drought; wherever wheat grows, oats can grow too. Main rabi fodders are berseem, lucerne, oats and ryegrass. Yield: easily 700 to 800 maunds of green fodder per acre; seed yield 20 to 25 maunds per acre.
aspects.varieties:
Approved varieties: Super Green Jai, Evergreen Jai, Sargodha Jai 2011, S-2000, Barkat, Faisalabad Oats-1, Faisalabad Oats-11, NARC Jai and PARC Jai. Evergreen stays green longer and has a strong stem, so it doesn't fall over (lodge). Punjab Jai is less affected by stem rot.
Seed rate: 32 kg per acre for fodder, 16 to 20 kg per acre for a seed crop. Mixed with berseem: 8 to 10 kg oats and 6 kg berseem per acre.
Use clean, weed-free seed; if chicory (kasni) is mixed in, soak seed in a 5 percent salt solution, remove floating seed and wash well before sowing. Seed is available from the Punjab Seed Corporation, Fodder Research Institute Sargodha, Regional Agricultural Research Institute Bahawalpur and Fodder Research Station Faisalabad.
aspects.sowing:
Soil: heavy loam. Plough and plank 3 to 4 times; laser levelling gives even, better growth.
Time: fodder crop early October to end November; seed-only crop 15 to 30 November.
Method: preferably in lines one foot apart; 1.5 feet apart for a seed crop.
Mixed with berseem: prepare the land, apply the recommended fertilizer, broadcast 8 to 10 kg oats per acre, plough and plank, make bunds for basins, irrigate, then broadcast 6 kg berseem per acre. The mix gives richer fodder from berseem's first two cuts, more yield and an earlier first cut.
An early crop cut for fodder at 60 to 65 days can still give a good seed crop from the regrowth.
aspects.fertilizer: Needs 46 kg nitrogen, 36 kg phosphorus and 12 kg potash per acre. At sowing: 1.5 bags DAP, half a bag of urea and half a bag of SOP. With the first irrigation: 1 bag of urea. If stem rot appears, reduce nitrogen; use potash and don't overuse nitrogen.
aspects.irrigation: Fodder crop: 3 to 4 irrigations including the pre-sowing one (rauni). First irrigation three weeks after sowing, then as needed. Seed crop: water especially at booting and during pollination for high yield. Avoid over-watering (stem rot).
aspects.pests_diseases:
Rule: never spray the crop meant for fodder. Spray only seed crops, or spray after cutting the fodder, in the morning or evening to protect bees. Nothing should be sprayed 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Armyworm (lashkari sundi): greenish-brown caterpillar with yellow stripes and two black spots behind the head; curls up when touched. From February–March it eats leaves down to the veins, plus flowers and buds. Don't spray full-grown caterpillars; wait until they pupate. Keep the crop weed-free, use light and sex-pheromone traps, and dig water-filled trenches with kerosene around badly hit fields so caterpillars can't move on. In severe attack, after cutting, spray per acre 50 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml lufenuron.
American bollworm: eats leaves; hay crops suffer most. If essential, cut the fodder and then spray per acre 40 ml spinosad, or 25 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml emamectin benzoate, or 200 ml lufenuron. Use light and pheromone traps; check seed crops and spray while caterpillars are young.
Looper (kubri sundi): green caterpillar that loops when moving; webs and eats tender leaves. Same rules: don't spray fodder, spray after cutting; trenches with kerosene around fields.
Whitefly (seed crop): sucks sap, leaves turn yellow with black sooty mould. Spray per acre 250 ml acetamiprid, or 400 ml flonicamid, or 500 ml pyriproxyfen.
Thrips (seed crop): suck sap so leaves dry. Spray 200 ml chlorfenapyr per acre, and use yellow or blue sticky traps.
Aphid (sust tela): dark green, sucks sap, sooty mould follows. Sow treated seed; never spray the fodder crop. On the seed crop spray per acre 200 ml imidacloprid or nitenpyram, or 250 ml acetamiprid or bifenthrin.
Shoot fly: enters and dries the shoots; in severe attack cut the fodder, then spray 200 ml imidacloprid or emamectin benzoate per acre.
Fodder weevil: larva and adult eat green leaf tissue and new shoots; cut the fodder early. On the seed crop spray 40 to 50 ml flubendiamide or chlorantraniliprole per acre.
Lygus and sting bugs: damage buds, flowers and green pods so flowers drop and seed shrivels, mostly in the seed crop. Spray a recommended insecticide.
Stem rot: use a lower seed rate, avoid over-watering, keep water from diseased fields away from healthy ones, rotate crops, use potash and don't overuse nitrogen. Punjab Jai (oats) is less affected.
aspects.weeds:
Rotating oats with other rabi crops helps control weeds.
Itsit: spray pendimethalin 1.5 litres per acre three weeks to a month before sowing and irrigate; plough at wattar and leave open.
Note: grass-killer sprays (such as quizalofop) are not for oats, because oats is itself a grass.
Do not hoe right after spraying: dust can carry the chemical into the farmer's body.
aspects.harvesting: Oats are cut between August and March, depending on sowing. An early crop cut for fodder at 60 to 65 days can regrow for seed. Oats can also be made into hay. No spray of any kind 20 to 25 days before cutting.
aspects.machinery: Use a laser land leveller for even growth.
aspects.other: Oats are often sown mixed with berseem for an earlier, bigger first cut.

timing.sowing: 1 October to 30 November (seed crop 15 to 30 November)
